reasoning: B wins narrowly, 6.4 to 6.2. Set B matches the ground truth closely. Every agent is scored against both a random player and a scripted bot. Everything runs on the laptop CPU with free tools. There are explicit ladders for value learning (table Q-learning, then DQN built rung by rung), for policy gradients (REINFORCE up to PPO) and for co-learning (both at once, taking turns, past versions, plus controls), so each concept the user named gets its own before-and-after lesson. B's weakness is the build front: its M1 plan was not updated after AD-16 and AD-17 changed the core to sides and schedules. The packets for M1-T01 (the interface task) and M1-T03 failed to generate because they read the retired `registry.make_agent`. The plan also has no tasks for the PL-01 steps `run_streams`, `make_schedule`, `SoloSchedule` and `test_lineup`, which `train_loop` now needs. The architecture also still carries process narration. Set A's M1 is coherent and its packets build. But it departs from the ground truth: there is no random baseline, and it adds a rented-GPU cost path (`usd_per_hour`, `device=cuda`, a $5 limit) and a library-twin comparison the user never asked for. It splits a solo learning lab into 13 packages, and its milestones include a twin-only leftover (M4) that is blocked on a probe. On balance, B's correct and complete design outweighs A's cleaner but off-target build plan, though B's first task cannot start until the plan is redone.
